correctAnswers: Acute, symptomatic ophthalmic artery occlusion, central retinal artery occlusion, or branch retinal artery occlusion within 24 hours
options: Acute, symptomatic ophthalmic artery occlusion, central retinal artery occlusion, or branch retinal artery occlusion within 24 hours
An asymptomatic retinal embolus without infarction identified during a routine examination
A newly diagnosed, asymptomatic central retinal artery occlusion arranged for prompt outpatient evaluation

candidates.rationale: Acute, symptomatic ophthalmic artery occlusion, central retinal artery occlusion, or branch retinal artery occlusion within 24 hours requires immediate stroke-center referral because acute retinal arterial ischemia is associated with stroke risk. Asymptomatic findings without infarction are described as requiring prompt evaluation rather than immediate referral.

correctAnswers: At the bifurcation of the common carotid artery into the internal and external carotid arteries
options: At the bifurcation of the common carotid artery into the internal and external carotid arteries
At the point where the central retinal artery divides into superior and inferior branches
Within the ophthalmic artery as it branches from the internal carotid artery
Along the external carotid artery after it has divided from the common carotid artery
candidates.rationale: Atheromatous plaque commonly forms at the bifurcation where the common carotid artery divides into the internal and external carotid arteries. This location can produce retinal emboli when a small plaque releases cholesterol material. The central retinal artery and ophthalmic artery locations are not the described carotid plaque site, and the external carotid artery after the bifurcation is less specific than the identified bifurcation location.

sourceCitations.quote: Commonly occurs at the bifurcation of the common carotid into the ICA and ECA

options: Valvular cardiac disease

A dull, elongated, highly mobile embolus
candidates.rationale: Calcific retinal emboli are associated with valvular cardiac disease. Atheromatous plaque, usually in the carotid, is associated with fibrin-platelet emboli, while the remaining choices describe embolus appearances or mobility rather than the stated source of calcific emboli.

Transient monocular and binocular visual loss occur with equal frequency

candidates.rationale: Systemic vascular causes of transient monocular vision loss include emboli, hypoperfusion, vasculitis, and hyperviscosity or hypercoagulable states. Ocular causes involve structures such as the tear film, cornea, retina, or optic nerve, whereas orbital causes include masses.

options: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the brain

candidates.rationale: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the brain is the recommended brain-imaging component of the evaluation for acute retinal ischemia. Carotid imaging, electrocardiography, and transthoracic echocardiography assess vascular or cardiac contributors, but they are not diffusion-weighted brain studies.

sourceCitations.quote:
Embolic eval (carotid, cardiac studies), GCA studies (> 50 years old), hematologic abnormalities

- Transthoracic Echocardiogram

Carotid and cardiac evaluations are also listed components of retinal arterial emboli work-up, but limiting the evaluation to either one would not address the specific association with a young patient lacking conventional risk factors.

options: Branch retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion
Ophthalmic artery occlusion
Transient monocular vision loss
candidates.rationale: Branch retinal artery occlusion involves one branch of the central retinal artery, so its effects can be limited to a sector or hemifield. The described pattern is consistent with the evidence that branch occlusion may produce sectoral or hemifield visual-field loss and that many patients retain visual acuity of 20/40 or better, especially when the macula is not involved.

sourceCitations.quote:
An occlusion of one of the branches of the CRA
  - May have sudden vision loss if there is macular involvement
    - Sometimes asymptomatic
    - Presenting VA: 75% of patients are 20/40 or better
    - Sectoral/hemi VF loss
